title: How Skyrim AI NPCs sent me down the rabbit hole
author: Lanfirus2
selftext:
Live long and prosper.  
I decided to start keeping notes on how I got to the point where AI convinced me to keep notes about the process of developing a game that actively uses AI as part of the gameplay. First things first.

# Neural networks and Skyrim

At first my attitude was basically, "Uh... so what?" That was a year or two ago. I didn't really need them, and they didn't seem much different from a search engine or specialized tools. So I forgot about them.  
At some point, while searching around on YouTube, I saw something like this:

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4vJGEGSvvbg](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4vJGEGSvvbg)

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sZgVl9-RXTQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sZgVl9-RXTQ)

And I'm quite the gamer and Skyrim fan. I started playing back in the last century, when I was about 7, on one of the first computers in town. And I have hundreds of hours in Skyrim (and yes - I've never finished the main quest and never made it to the end of the game :) ).

The idea seemed awesome to me. Skyrim is already full of events and ridiculous shit on its own. And now there was another layer of fun and madness - bringing NPCs to life with AI.

Naturally, I immediately wanted to play something like that myself. It wasn't hard to figure out, I tried a couple of options and settled on SkyrimNet. You can either pay and enjoy yourself - everything is basically ready, just keep topping up the balance and go - or you can mess around with it and save a lot of money. And if you're playing in a language other than English, you can also improve the capabilities quite a bit.

# Optimizing SkyrimNet

Since I obviously didn't want to pay a lot of money, I started optimizing the process. Some things can't really be avoided. Network LLMs are necessary for parsing player input, making difficult decisions, producing a coherent response, and some other things (for example, generating video, audio, etc.).

Everything else can, in principle, be moved to your own computer, to your own local neural networks. If your hardware can handle it.  
For Skyrim specifically, the first things that make sense to move locally are TTS and STT.

STT means Speech-to-text, converting voice input into text. In other words, I say into the microphone, "Hey, Lydia. Will you carry my load today?" and exactly that text, or something very close to it, should appear on the screen. Or disappear into the depths of SkyrimNet.  
This is very easy and very cheap to solve in terms of computer resources. There are tons of small neural networks designed specifically for this. For English and other languages. The only question is finding one that works for you. How exactly that particular model recognizes your particular voice and speaking style in your particular language.

TTS means Text-to-speech, converting text into voice. In other words, Lydia answers my question with, "Fuck off! Carry your own load." and I hear it with my own ears. If everything is done properly, I'll hear it in Lydia's own voice, the same voice she uses for her lines in the game.  
And this is where the kind of sexual adventures started that completely changed how I saw modern neural networks.

# Messing around with TTS

The possibility of being told to fuck off by any guard or bum in Skyrim seemed divine to me. And it's one of the most expensive pleasures if you use external neural-network services. So this was the very first candidate for moving onto my own computer. SkyrimNet even lets you do that pretty much out of the box. But, as in that joke, there's a nuance.

In the version of SkyrimNet I was using, the only TTS you could set up without problems was English. It had, apparently, 2 built-in neural networks that worked properly only with English text. If you tried to voice, for example, Russian text, you got some insane letter-by-letter reading or some other form of madness. And there was no way to change that. The neural networks were built into SkyrimNet itself, and SkyrimNet was distributed already compiled, without source code.  
Of those two models, one was extremely fast but had literally 4-5 voice options, while the other was slower but apparently could speak in any voice using a sample.

I didn't want to give up, so as usual I went looking for another way. SkyrimNet provides an endpoint for a certain type of TTS neural network that you can connect to. I downloaded something similar, connected it, tried it - it works. But kind of like shit. The voice quality isn't great, and the time between my question and the NPC's answer feels like forever - 10-20 seconds.

# And this is where the tank's turret got blown off

That's from a joke, by the way, and here it symbolizes the beginning of major romantic adventures with everything in sight and a steady stream of carefully selected profanity.  
It turned out that finding the right neural network for this job is really not easy.  
The model needs to meet at least these requirements:

* Use a reasonable amount of resources while running. VRAM first and foremost. My GPU has 16 GB, and I figured it was safe to allocate about 8 GB to a model like this.
* Reproduce Russian properly (in my case; yours might be some other language). And this is where things get bad. A lot of models claim to support various languages. But when you actually start testing them, the circus begins:
   * Not at all
   * You can understand what it's saying, but with some horrible accent. Usually either Chinese or some kind of Caucasus accent.
   * Intelligibility is fine, but the intonation is a mess
* Be able to work from a voice example and generate audio from a 5-10 second sample
* Be able to work in streaming mode. Any model can wait until the whole line arrives and then synthesize the entire thing. Except that guarantees 10+ seconds. At that point it's no longer a game, it's torture. And you can forget combat banter entirely. Streaming lets the model start generating audio from the first chunks of text without waiting for the whole line. The hard part is keeping the intonation right when the TTS simply doesn't know the rest of the text yet.

To be continued
